title: Configuration-based understanding of superradiant phase transitions in Dicke lattices
abstract: The emergence of multiple superradiant phases in Dicke lattice models has attracted considerable attention in the quantum optics community. However, a unified understanding of the origin of multistability and its relation to different superradiant phases is still lacking. Here, we develop a configuration-based understanding to classify the superradiant phases in Dicke lattices. We show that photon hopping naturally organizes the possible superradiant configurations according to the lattice symmetry, providing a unified interpretation of the nonequilibrium phase diagram and the emergence of multistability. For the dissipative four-site Dicke lattice, we obtain the complete phase diagram and identify the coexistence of up to four stable superradiant phases. The proposed classification is further extended to five- and six-site lattices. Moreover, we demonstrate that the same configuration-based understanding also applies to the closed Dicke lattice, where the ground state uniquely selects one of the allowed configurations. Finally, we show that different configurations may belong to either same or distinct nonequilibrium universality classes in the dissipative Dicke lattice, while they share the same equilibrium universality class in the closed Dicke lattice. Our results provide a unified picture for understanding equilibrium and nonequilibrium superradiant phase transitions in Dicke lattices.
summary: The paper introduces a novel configuration-based framework to unify the understanding of superradiant phase transitions in Dicke lattices. By classifying possible stable configurations based on lattice symmetry, it explains the emergence of multistability in dissipative systems. This unified picture successfully bridges the gap between nonequilibrium steady states and equilibrium ground states.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a unified, configuration-based understanding of how multistability arises in superradiant phase transitions within Dicke lattices.
main_result: It successfully classifies multiple stable superradiant phases based on lattice symmetry and demonstrates that the classification framework applies consistently across both dissipative (nonequilibrium) and closed (equilibrium) regimes.
method: The analysis employs mean-field approximations, deriving semiclassical equations of motion for stability analysis in the dissipative case, and minimizing energy functionals for the equilibrium case.
model_or_system: The system is the Dicke lattice model, involving coupled atom-resonator units on a 1D lattice. The dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation (dissipative) or analyzed via Hamiltonian minimization (closed).
key_observables: Order parameters characterizing superradiant phases (e.g., real photonic component $R_j$), ground-state energy ($E_{GS}$), and excitation gaps ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($g$), photon hopping parameter ($\xi$), cavity decay rate ($\kappa$), and lattice size ($N=4$ analyzed in detail).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mean-field approximation, factorizing operator correlations $\langle AB angle \simeq \langle A angle \langle B angle$, and using the Discrete Truncated Wigner Approximation (DTWA) for dissipative dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing regions of multistability (up to fourfold for $N=4$) in the dissipative case, alongside plots detailing ground-state energy and excitation gaps versus coupling strength.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the model and develops a configuration classification scheme. It then analyzes the dissipative system using steady-state solutions and stability analysis to map out the nonequilibrium phase diagram. Finally, it compares these findings with the equilibrium case (closed lattice) to establish a unified picture.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful topological/combinatorial tool—the configuration classification—to organize complex non-equilibrium phase diagrams in quantum optics models like the Dicke lattice, unifying disparate physical regimes.
